[Module 4](/learn/modules/04-ai-infrastructure/) argues that model choice is a routing decision and
that the cost-latency-quality triangle should be measured rather than assumed. This lab does the
measuring, and the answer was not what the lab was originally written to show.

Source: [`labs/model-router`](https://github.com/vins13pattar/principal-ai-engineer-handbook/tree/main/labs/model-router)

<Aside type="caution" title="production-shaped, not production-ready">
  No model is ever called. Correctness comes from a seeded hash so results are reproducible; costs
  and quality figures are lab fixtures chosen for their relative ordering, not any vendor's pricing
  and not benchmark results. Latency is not modelled at all — the triangle has three corners and
  this lab measures two. Health, retries, and outages are
  [`async-ai-gateway`](/build/labs/async-ai-gateway/)'s job.
</Aside>

## Not the same routing as the gateway

[`async-ai-gateway`](/build/labs/async-ai-gateway/) routes between *replicas of equivalent
providers* by observed success rate — a health problem. This lab routes between *models of
different capability and price* by what the task needs. Both are called routing; they share almost
no logic, and the labs are kept apart so each stays about one thing.

## The path a task takes

<Mermaid code={routingPath} title="Capability filtering first, policy second, and an escalation branch that bills for both calls" />

## The finding

Escalation — try the cheap model, fall back to the expensive one when it looks unsure — is standard
advice, and the intuition is that it saves money while holding quality. **The first version of this
lab's test suite asserted exactly that, and it failed.**

Over a fixed 200-task workload, with a *perfect* confidence signal — low exactly when the answer is
wrong, the best case any escalation policy could hope for:

| | Cheap only | Escalating |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correct | 166 / 200 | 197 / 200 |
| Total cost | 0.040 | 0.550 |
| Cost per correct answer | 0.00024 | **0.00279** |

Accuracy up 19%. Cost per correct answer **11× worse**. And it is not an artefact of the 75× price
gap between those tiers — the relationship holds at 10×, 5×, and 2×.

The cause is arithmetic rather than modelling. A cheap model already right 83% of the time
contributes a large number of cheap correct answers; escalation adds a smaller number of expensive
ones, so the average can only move upward. **Cost per correct answer is a trap metric here, and it
is the one everybody reaches for.**

## The number that actually decides

What escalation buys is *marginal* correct answers, so the honest question is what each rescued
answer cost:

```text
marginal cost per rescued answer
  = (escalated_cost − baseline_cost) / (escalated_correct − baseline_correct)
```

About 0.00044 per rescued answer at a 2× price ratio; about 0.016 at 75×. Whether either is worth
paying depends on what a wrong answer costs you — a product question, and one the router should not
pretend to answer. `test_marginal_cost_per_rescued_answer_scales_with_the_cost_ratio` pins the
relationship so the conclusion cannot quietly invert.

## What else the tests pin

**Capability filtering happens before cost.** `small` is the cheapest model in the fleet and cannot
write code. A router sorting by price first picks it and is cheap, fast, and wrong.

**A quality floor nothing clears falls back visibly.** The router still returns a decision — you
cannot serve nothing — but records in the reason string that the floor was not met, so a bar nobody
is hitting is auditable rather than invisible.

**A budget cap raises instead of downgrading.** Silently choosing a worse model to stay under budget
is a quality regression with no alert attached.

**Ties break on name, not registration order.** A router whose choice depends on dict iteration
produces cost reports nobody can reconcile between runs.

**The confidence signal's usefulness is invisible in the API.** Swapping an informative signal for a
meaningless one changes nothing a type checker or a code review would catch — escalation still
fires, still bills twice, and returns far less. That is why it has to be measured.

## Run it

```bash
cd labs/model-router
uv venv .venv && uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e '.[dev]'
./.venv/bin/python -m ruff check . && ./.venv/bin/python -m mypy src && ./.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q
```

16 tests, `ruff` clean, `mypy --strict` clean.

## Principal-level discussion points

- **What is a wrong answer worth?** Until that number exists, no escalation policy can be justified
  or rejected — and most teams adopt one without ever asking.
- **Who owns `ModelSpec.quality`?** It is a static claim here. In production it decays, and a router
  optimising against stale quality numbers degrades silently.
- **Capability declarations are trust.** A model that claims it can `reason` and cannot will be
  routed work it fails at, cheaply and confidently.
- **The triangle's third corner.** Escalation spends latency as well as money. A task that escalates
  takes two round trips and may miss a deadline the single expensive call would have met.
